summary: Describes Tetrys, an experimental on-the-fly network coding protocol for delay-sensitive and loss-sensitive data over lossy networks. It can recover from lost packets with coded packets without waiting a round trip. It is a product of the Coding for Efficient NetWork Communications Research Group.

plainLanguage.summary: Extra puzzle pieces are sent along with the real ones, so if one gets lost the receiver can rebuild it without asking for a resend.

questions: how tetrys recovers from packet loss
subtitle: An on-the-fly network coding protocol for loss-sensitive, delay-sensitive streaming.

tldr.problem: Real-time and delay-sensitive applications over lossy networks need to recover from packet loss without waiting for retransmission, which introduces unacceptable delays.
tldr.mechanism: Tetrys uses an elastic encoding window to generate coded packets on-the-fly as linear combinations of source packets over a finite field. The sender receives feedback about received packets and shrinks the window, while coded packets allow the receiver to recover losses by solving linear systems.
tldr.outcome: Delay-sensitive applications can recover from packet loss within one round-trip time instead of waiting for retransmission, improving quality of experience for streaming video, VoIP, and interactive applications over lossy networks.

facts.label: Finite fields supported
facts.value: GF(2^4) with 16 elements, GF(2^8) with 256 elements

facts.label: Decoding algorithm
facts.value: Gaussian elimination over the finite field

today: RFC 9407 is an Experimental protocol published in June 2023. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It represents the experience gained by researchers in network coding and is available for experimental implementations and evaluation in real-world conditions.

sections.title: Network Coding for Real-Time Streaming
sections.content:
Network coding is a technique where routers and hosts combine packets mathematically rather than simply forwarding them unchanged. Tetrys applies network coding to single-flow, real-time streaming scenarios where delay-sensitive applications cannot afford to wait for retransmitted packets.

Traditional error recovery uses retransmission: when a packet is lost, the receiver detects the loss and requests the packet be sent again. This introduces an extra round-trip time of delay, which is unacceptable for video conferencing, online gaming, and other interactive applications. Tetrys instead sends coded packets—packets that are linear combinations of source packets over a finite field. If a source packet is lost, the receiver can recover it from the coded packets using Gaussian elimination, without waiting for a retransmission.

The key innovation of Tetrys is the elastic encoding window. Rather than collecting source packets into fixed blocks before encoding (as in traditional Forward Error Correction), Tetrys continuously generates coded packets from an elastic window of unacknowledged source packets. This reduces encoding delay and allows the sender to adapt the redundancy level based on feedback from the receiver about which packets have been received.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for a replacement, the receiver gets mathematical combinations of packets. With enough combinations, it can rebuild a lost packet on the spot.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Architecture
sections.content:
A Tetrys system consists of a sender with a Tetrys encoder and a receiver with a Tetrys decoder, connected by a lossy network. The sender's application provides source packets (source symbols) to the encoder. The encoder maintains an elastic encoding window containing all unacknowledged source packets. When the sender needs to transmit data, it can either send a source packet as-is or generate a coded packet.

A coded packet is created by choosing an encoding vector—a set of finite-field coefficients that weight each source packet in the window. The coded packet is the sum of (coefficient multiplied by source packet) for all packets in the window. Each coded packet includes the encoding vector so the receiver knows which source packets were combined and with what coefficients.

The receiver decodes packets as they arrive. Source packets are directly decoded. When a coded packet arrives, the receiver records it. As packets accumulate, the receiver solves a system of linear equations over the finite field. When the rank of the system is sufficient, the receiver can recover any lost source packets. The receiver sends feedback packets back to the sender indicating which source packets have been received or decoded, allowing the sender to remove them from the encoding window.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender creates puzzle pieces: some are real packets, others are mathematical blends of real packets. The receiver collects them and uses the blends to rebuild missing pieces.

sections.title: Encoding and the Elastic Window
sections.content:
At the start of a transmission, the Tetrys encoder chooses an initial code rate that adds redundancy, since it does not yet know the packet loss rate. In steady state, when the encoder receives a source packet from the application, it may generate coded packets according to the configured or dynamically adjusted code rate.

The encoder uses a Coding Coefficient Generator (CCGI) to deterministically derive the coefficients in the encoding vector. Two finite fields are supported: GF(2^4) with 16 elements and GF(2^8) with 256 elements. Choosing 16 elements reduces encoding complexity; choosing 256 elements improves erasure recovery performance. The CCGI is included in each coded packet so the decoder can regenerate the same coefficients.

The elastic encoding window has a maximum size that limits the complexity of the linear combinations. When a new source packet arrives and the window is full, the oldest packet is discarded, and the new packet is added. As the receiver sends feedback indicating which packets have been received or decoded, the sender removes those packets from the window, shrinking it and making room for new packets. This feedback-driven window management keeps the encoding complexity manageable even during long transmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a sliding window of recent packets. For each outgoing packet, it mixes some of the packets in the window using a mathematical recipe. When the receiver confirms it got a packet, the sender slides the window forward.

sections.title: Decoding and Loss Recovery
sections.content:
At the receiver, each arriving packet is either a source packet or a coded packet. Source packets directly provide data to the application. Coded packets are stored along with their encoding vectors in a decoding buffer.

The decoding process uses Gaussian elimination over the finite field to solve a system of linear equations. Each coded packet represents one equation: coded_value = coefficient_1 * source_1 + coefficient_2 * source_2 + ... In matrix form, if the encoder created coded packets from source packets with indices [1, 2, 3] and [2, 3, 4], and if packets 1, 3, and the first coded packet arrive but packet 2 is lost, the receiver can solve for packet 2.

The decoder works on-the-fly: as each coded packet arrives, the decoder attempts to add it to the linear system and solves for any unknown source packets if the system has sufficient rank. Recovered source packets are immediately delivered to the application or the decoding buffer. This on-the-fly recovery reduces the decoding delay compared to techniques that wait for a complete block of packets before decoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver treats the blended packets like math equations. When it has enough equations, it can solve for the missing packets using algebra.

sections.title: Packet Formats and Signaling
sections.content:
Tetrys defines three packet types with a common header format inspired by the Layered Coding Transport (LCT) protocol. Source packets carry a source symbol ID and the payload. Coded packets carry a coded symbol ID, the encoding vector (which identifies which source packets were combined and their coefficients), and the coded payload. Window update packets are feedback messages sent from the receiver to the sender, indicating which source packets have been received or decoded.

The encoding vector is flexible and compressed to reduce overhead. It can store source symbol IDs as a full list, as compressed edge blocks (for consecutive IDs like [1..3] stored as two boundaries), or omit ID information entirely if sender and receiver agree on the set of source packets in the window. Coefficients are stored as 4-bit or 8-bit values depending on the finite field used. Padding aligns all fields to 32-bit boundaries.

The common header includes space for congestion control information and a transport session identifier, allowing Tetrys to coexist with other transport mechanisms. The header length field enables parsing of extensions and the payload, making the format compatible with other protocols like FECFRAME and NORM.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet says what kind it is, which recipes were used to blend it (if it's blended), and how long the message is. The receiver uses this information to figure out which packets match up.
